relationships.description: The installed platform software reads or writes the file, image, script or configuration document at runtime, as when a database engine loads its config file or a container runtime pulls and unpacks an image.
relationships.evidence: The software's startup command, service unit or mounted volume references the artifact's path, or its logs show it loading or writing that file or image digest.

relationships.description: The platform product is the active element that carries out the ongoing infrastructure behavior, such as a PostgreSQL instance performing streaming replication or an NGINX process performing load balancing.
relationships.evidence: The product's configuration enables the feature that embodies the function, for example replication settings in postgresql.conf or an upstream block in nginx.conf.

relationships.description: The artifact is an integral constituent of this specific software installation, such as its binaries, bundled plugins or instance-specific configuration, and has no purpose outside it.
relationships.evidence: The installation manifest, package file list or Dockerfile layer shows the artifact being installed into the software's own directory tree as part of that product's distribution.

relationships.description: The software cannot run without the physical hardware it is installed on or that it drives, such as an operating system on a bare-metal server or a storage engine on a specific disk array.
relationships.evidence: The hardware inventory, provisioning playbook or CMDB record lists the software as installed on that device's serial or asset tag, or its configuration binds to the device's disks or interfaces.

relationships.description: The dependent platform software requires the other product to be installed and running in order to function, such as a language runtime needing an operating system or a broker needing a coordination service.
relationships.evidence: A package dependency declaration, base image in a Dockerfile, or the software's configuration pointing to the other product's endpoint shows the required prerequisite.

relationships.description: The platform product is the concrete mechanism that puts the recorded security control into effect, such as a web application firewall enforcing input filtering or a database engine providing encryption at rest.
relationships.evidence: The product's configuration enables the control's settings (e.g. TLS enforcement, WAF rule set, encryption keys) and the threat model lists this product as the countermeasure's implementation.

relationships.description: The choice and configuration of the platform product embody a general architectural principle, such as using a managed open-source database to honor a 'prefer open standards' principle.
relationships.evidence: An architecture decision record or technology radar entry cites the principle as the rationale for selecting or configuring this product.

relationships.description: The platform product reduces the likelihood or impact of the modeled attack, as when a reverse proxy's rate limiting blunts credential stuffing or an OS hardening profile limits privilege escalation.
relationships.evidence: The threat model entry names the product as a mitigating element and its configuration contains the protective setting addressing that attack technique.

relationships.description: The platform product opens the concrete access point, such as a listening port, socket or broker listener, through which consumers reach its capabilities.
relationships.evidence: The product's configuration declares the listener (e.g. port 5432 in postgresql.conf or listeners in Kafka server.properties) and a container or service definition exposes that port.

relationships.description: The off-the-shelf product directly delivers the externally visible application behavior without custom code, as when a search engine product is the realization of a 'Product Search' application service.
relationships.evidence: The service catalog or architecture documentation maps the application service to this product, and consumers' API calls are routed straight to the product's endpoints.

relationships.description: The platform product is the means by which a business-facing service is actually delivered, such as a hosted email server realizing a 'Customer Correspondence' business service.
relationships.evidence: Business service documentation or a service catalog entry lists the product as the delivering technology, with no intermediate application component in between.

relationships.description: Adopting and operating the platform product brings about the stakeholders' intended end state, such as a clustered database realizing a goal of higher availability.
relationships.evidence: A roadmap, business case or decision record states that introducing this product is the means of achieving the named goal.

relationships.description: The platform product evaluates and enforces the policy's ordered rules to reach access decisions, such as an authorization server or API gateway executing a named access-control policy.
relationships.evidence: The product's policy configuration (e.g. OPA bundle, gateway policy file, database role grants) contains the rules of the named policy in its defined priority order.

relationships.description: The platform product is what actually delivers the infrastructure capability consumers rely on, such as Redis realizing the caching service or RabbitMQ realizing the messaging service.
relationships.evidence: Infrastructure-as-code or the platform service catalog provisions this product as the backing implementation of the named technology service.

relationships.description: The selected product and version stays within a mandated restriction, such as an approved-technology list, a licensing limit or a data-residency rule.
relationships.evidence: The product appears on the approved technology list or its deployment region and license terms recorded in configuration match those required by the constraint's decision record.

relationships.description: The platform product as configured delivers the verifiable property the requirement demands, such as a database engine providing point-in-time recovery or a broker guaranteeing at-least-once delivery.
relationships.evidence: A requirements traceability matrix links the requirement to this product, and its configuration or acceptance test results demonstrate the required behavior.

relationships.description: The platform product provides hosting, runtime, storage or messaging capability that the application component relies on, such as the JVM running a service or PostgreSQL storing its data.
relationships.evidence: The component's Dockerfile base image, connection string, dependency manifest or deployment descriptor references the product or its endpoint.

relationships.description: The platform product directly supports execution of the business activities, such as a workflow engine product or document management server used throughout a claims-handling process.
relationships.evidence: Process documentation or BPMN deployment metadata shows the process running on, or its steps relying on, this product.

relationships.description: The platform product supplies capability that another infrastructure function relies on, such as a time-sync daemon serving the log rotation function or a key store serving a replication function.
relationships.evidence: The function's configuration or scripts invoke the product's commands, sockets or APIs to perform their work.

relationships.description: The platform product's behavior causes the discrete infrastructure state change, such as a database engine emitting a failover event or a container runtime signalling a container exit.
relationships.evidence: The product's logs, event stream or alerting configuration shows it emitting the named event (e.g. a Kubernetes event, systemd notification or replication failover hook).

relationships.description: The platform product sends and receives its traffic over the network, such as a database cluster attached to a private VPC subnet or a broker reachable over a corporate LAN.
relationships.evidence: The product's bind address, host network interface or infrastructure-as-code declaration places it in the network's address range or subnet.

relationships.description: The platform product communicates with a specific peer over the logical link, such as a database replica streaming WAL over a dedicated replication connection or a broker bridging to a remote site through a VPN tunnel.
relationships.evidence: The product's configuration names the remote peer endpoint of the path (e.g. primary_conninfo, shovel or federation upstream URI, tunnel interface).

notes: composes artifact is questionable: artifacts normally realize system software (ArchiMate), and overlaps accesses. realizes business service and realizes goal skip layers; goal is better served by supports. implements principle should likely be governed-by-principles. serves vs assigned-to technologyfunction may confuse modelers. implements countermeasure and mitigates threat largely duplicate each other.
